  (d) The SAME posture WITH an approval row present is ALSO ADMITTED, because an approval is additional authority and never a disqualifier, but the row is still validated when present, so one that does not cover this intent is refused with details.reason 'mismatch' (different action_class or resource), 'terminal' (status executed or rejected) or 'expired' (expires_at <= nowIso). Rule (d) exists because approving a class the seed calibrates autonomous is a real case, and leaving it undefined is how a wrong write happens in the highest-risk slice in the project.
  (e) ANY other posture ('approval-required', 'shadow', or the fail-closed no-row default) admits ONLY with an approval row present, unexpired at nowIso, non-terminal, and matching intent.action_class and intent.resource; otherwise the refusal names the failing condition 'no-approval', 'expired', 'terminal' or 'mismatch'. 'shadow' is IN this rule deliberately: shadow means NEVER AUTONOMOUS, not never possible. A human approval is the whole point of the approvals queue, and a reading in which a shadow-pinned class can never be approved makes the queue a dead end for the highest-risk class the product knows. IAC-4 asks that new-geography 'stays in shadow or approval', which is exactly this split.
  (f) THE MICRO-LIMIT, THEN THE BAND. MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED when the intent's amount exceeds the class microLimitMicros, where the amount is constraints.delta_micros when it is a finite number and 0 otherwise. THE COMPARISON FOR A CLASS THAT DOES NOT REQUIRE A MICROS CONSTRAINT IS STATED BECAUSE A CRITERION RESTS ON IT: an absent constraints.delta_micros is 0 and the check is 0 <= microLimitMicros, so campaign-status with an empty constraints object is admitted, while a NEGATIVE delta_micros is MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED on every class regardless of the flag. For budget-change, whose requiresMicrosConstraint is true, an absent, non-numeric, negative or non-integer delta_micros is ALSO MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, because a missing number is not a small number and an absent constraint otherwise passes an upper-bound check by not existing.

RULE (f)'s BAND IS A FLOOR AND ITS DIRECTION IS NOT NEGOTIABLE. The intent's band is policyBand(maturity).label and the class's requiredMaturityBand is the LOWEST band permitted to act: admit iff BAND_ORDER.indexOf(actual) >= BAND_ORDER.indexOf(required), where BAND_ORDER = ['emergency-only','protective','moderate','strategic'] and labelFor(band) is exported alongside. policyBand is IMPORTED from src/domain/measurement.js rather than restated, and BAND_ORDER is the order its <0.35 / <0.70 / <0.90 edges already encode, so the gate and the metric surface cannot drift apart. A HIGHER band NEVER blocks: a class requiring 'protective' is ADMITTED at maturity 0.95, and a class requiring 'strategic' is refused for every maturity below 0.90, which coincides with policyBand's own gated flag. maturity 0.90 exactly is 'strategic' and is admitted, matching test/domain/measurement.test.js:106. A CEILING reading inverts the safety property: it would admit data at maturity 0 that the class declared too immature and refuse data at 0.95 that it declared ready. Note the doc drift, do not inherit it: docs/trd.md's TR-7 line writes '>0.90 strategic' where src/domain/measurement.js:244-259 and its pinned test say '>= 0.90'. The implementation wins, docs/ is out of bounds from a ticket branch, and the drift is filed in out_of_scope.

THE MATURITY ARGUMENT IS VALIDATED BEFORE IT IS USED, AND null IS ONE OF THE BAD VALUES. Anything that is not a finite number (undefined, null, NaN, a numeric string) is refused MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED with details {required, actual: null, maturity: null, reason: 'maturity-unknown'} BEFORE policyBand is called. null is explicitly in that set because the route's own computation substitutes 0 for a tenant with no events, and laundering 'no evidence' into a legitimate 0 is the same fail-open by a different door. maturity is a caller-supplied number and never an internal read: this module never touches a repository or a clock, so the ROUTE that supplies it owns the source and the doc comment says so.

issueCapability(intent, {secret, policyVersion, ttlMs, nowIso, expiresAtCap, nonce}) signs with node:crypto createHmac and returns {tenant, resource, action, constraints, maturity, band, expiry, nonce, policy_version} plus a capability_id, with expiry = min(now + ttlMs, expiresAtCap) and ttlMs 900_000. THE ENVELOPE CARRIES maturity AND band because they are properties of the gate decision and signing them is what makes the receipt's audit columns trustworthy: the executor copies them onto the action_records row, so the receipt records the band that was actually enforced on BOTH the autonomous and the approval path rather than null on the autonomous one. nonce is OPTIONAL and generated internally ('nce_' + 16 hex from randomUUID) only when omitted, which is what lets the decide route pass decisionNonce(approvalId) instead of a string it assembles itself.

validateCapability(capability, {secret, nowIso, killSwitches, nonces}) -> MALFORMED_CAPABILITY, BAD_SIGNATURE, EXPIRED_CAPABILITY, REPLAYED_NONCE, OVER_SCOPE (details name the violated constraint), KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE. Both injected ports are NON-MUTATING and read-only: killSwitches {isActive(tenantId, scope, scopeId)} and nonces {seen(tenantId, nonce)} where seen is never claim, because claiming a nonce is the executor's job and this module must never reserve one. createKernel({secret, policyVersion, ttlMs, killSwitches, nonces}) binds the ports and has the routes as their only callers. THE nonces PORT IS BOUND TO action_records, NOT TO capabilities: action_records carries UNIQUE (tenant_id, nonce) and holds a row only after a successful write, so seen is false for a freshly issued capability and true only for a nonce already spent. Binding it to capabilities would make seen true for every capability and validateCapability would answer REPLAYED_NONCE on every execution. REPLAYED_NONCE is therefore defence in depth that the executor's earlier dedupe shadows on the live path; the doc comment says so, and no one should 'fix' the duplicate answer into a 409 to make the branch reachable.

THE KILL-SWITCH CHECK, EXPLICITLY, because leaving it implicit is what made KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE and OVER_SCOPE unobservable: validateCapability evaluates FOUR scope keys, in this order, and refuses on the FIRST active one with details {scope, scope_id}. The keys are, and every one is derivable from the signed envelope with nothing added to it: ('global', envelope.tenant) - a global freeze is stored under the tenant that raised it, never under a '' sentinel - ('tenant', envelope.tenant), ('provider', 'meta_ads') - the sole provider this epic integrates, named as a constant here so the string is written once - and ('campaign', envelope.resource). A write is refused if any of the four is active, so a provider-wide freeze blocks a campaign write and a campaign-wide freeze blocks only that campaign. OVER_SCOPE is the sibling refusal and is what keeps a tenant's envelope from being executed against another tenant's resource: it is the combination of envelope.tenant not matching the caller's tenantId and a scope check that the envelope names. POSTURE_LABELS maps the three machine postures to the display strings the page renders and the criterion quotes: 'autonomous under micro-limits', 'approval required', 'shadow'.

Pure, no IO, no repository import. scoreFor(row) over a stored ledger row {evaluated, correct, needless, downside_penalties} and postureFor(actionClass, row, roster, pinned) -> 'autonomous-under-micro-limits' | 'approval-required' | 'shadow', with documented thresholds: autonomous requires evaluated >= 3 for that class AND precision (correct/evaluated) >= 0.90 AND false-intervention rate (needless/evaluated) <= 0.05 AND downside_penalties === 0. A pinned flag forces 'shadow' regardless of score, and a class with NO row is 'approval-required' (TR-24, fail closed), which is the only other path to that label and the reason the campaign-launch row of the table carries the 'no evidence' Why copy. recordOutcome(row, {outcome, needless, downside}) folds one evaluation into the next row. The two callers are the approvals page's posture table and kernel.validateIntent, both calling this one function, so the displayed posture and the enforced posture cannot disagree. The executor does NOT call it and must not: a signed capability is the attestation, and re-deriving posture at execute time would let a later trust-row edit retroactively invalidate a correctly issued capability.

createExecutor({repositories, provider, kernel, auditClock}). The ONLY module that calls a provider write method. execute(capability, {actor, tenantId}) runs its checks in THIS ORDER and the order is the contract.

(0) TENANT. The capability's own tenant field must equal the caller's tenantId, else {executed:false, error:{code:'TENANT_MISMATCH'}} with no write; the envelope is bearer material and the executor does not take the caller's word for it.

(1) DURABLE DEDUPE FIRST, in two sub-steps. (1a) If actionRecords.getByNonce(tenantId, nonce) already holds a row, return {executed:false, duplicate:true, receipt_id, reconciliation, drift} immediately, without validating through the kernel and without calling the provider; a duplicate mutates nothing, so it returns its receipt even while a kill switch is active. Stated in the doc comment so nobody 'fixes' it into a 409, because a second tab or a retried POST is exactly the case where a 409 tells the operator their action failed when it succeeded. (1b) ATOMIC CLAIM, repositories.idempotency.claim(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before the provider call, using the primitive the repository already ships (:133-172, whose claim is INSERT OR IGNORE and so genuinely atomic, and the shape src/workflows/scheduler.js:71-79 already uses), so of two interleaved deliveries exactly one reaches the provider; a false return means another caller won, so return {executed:false, duplicate:false, error:{code:'EXECUTION_IN_PROGRESS', retryable:true}} with NO provider call and NO wait. Step 1a alone is check-then-act and does not close the two-tab race; 1b is what makes that claim true. The loser is told to retry rather than to wait on a receipt row, because a winner that then FAILS releases the claim (below) and no row is ever coming - a bounded wait on a row that may never appear is the trap this replaces.

(2) kernel.validateCapability, where the signature, expiry, scope, replay and kill-switch rejections happen, the last over the four scope keys named in the kernel entry. ANY REFUSAL HERE, AND ANY REFUSAL FROM (0), RELEASES the 1b CLAIM through repositories.idempotency.release(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before returning. Nothing that did not reach the provider may leave a nonce burned.

(3) Resolve the write method from the capability's SIGNED action through the contract module's ACTION_WRITES map, never from anything the caller passes at execute time, and derive its arguments from the envelope through ONE named function, writeArgsFor(action, envelope). resource supplies the target id for update and status actions - the adset id for update_campaign_budget, the campaign id for set_campaign_status and update_campaign_creative. For create_campaign the resource is a PROPOSED id that does not exist yet and the name comes from envelope.constraints.name, NOT from resource: createCampaign takes {name} and mints its own id, so reading the name off resource would create a campaign literally called 'campaign_004'. constraints supply delta_micros for the budget action and the target status for the status action. This is stated because a previous revision left the mapping unsaid and an implementer then wrote a create against a resource the fake's fixtures do not contain. The SAME provider instance serves the write and the re-read in (4), so one request reconciles against the state it just wrote.

(4) Re-read provider state through the read interface. drift is classified: 'none' when the re-read agrees with the request and the provider reported no drift, otherwise the source the provider itself reports - 'manual', 'platform' or 'third-party'. reconciliation is a CLOSED VOCABULARY with the same treatment, because the receipt column, the toast and the failure panel all render it and only one of its values was ever named: 'agreed' when the post-write re-read reports exactly the requested state, 'diverged' when the re-read succeeded and reports something else, 'partial' when only some of a multi-field change landed, and 'unknown' when there is no re-read to compare against. The success path therefore yields 'agreed' on seeded data, which is the string qa_script step 3 and the successful-approve test case quote; 'unknown' is the provider-refusal value and the only one that reaches the failure panel. The fake reports drift only from a writeDrift option the tests inject, so 'none' is the only drift value reachable in a live QA run; that is filed in residual_risks rather than implied to be covered.

(5) Append the action_records receipt (repositories.actionRecords.append), record the idempotency effect, append an audit event carrying actor and capability id, and return {executed:true, receipt_id, requested, reported, reconciliation, drift}. THE RECEIPT COPIES maturity AND band FROM THE ENVELOPE onto maturity_at_decision and band_at_decision, which is why those columns are signed rather than recomputed: without this the two audit columns are null on every autonomous receipt and the receipt cannot answer which band was enforced.

A provider refusal (ok:false) RELEASES the claim through repositories.idempotency.release, returns {executed:false, duplicate:false, error, reconciliation:'unknown'}, writes NO action_records row and claims no nonce durably, so the caller's approval stays pending and a retry is a genuine retry rather than a swallowed claim. The provider is injected per request; the executor never constructs one. This module does not import trust.js and does not consult the ledger: a signed capability is the attestation and the gate has one owner.

Three exported pure functions and two effects, all over deterministic fixtures.

DETECTORS. spendSpike(fixture, {nowIso}) compares observed spend micros over the window against the seeded baseline; trackingLoss(fixture, {nowIso}) reports no qualified event past STALE_THRESHOLD_HOURS, IMPORTED from src/domain/measurement.js:242 and not restated; evaluate(fixture, {nowIso}) dispatches on kind and returns {tripped, kind, details}. The two fixtures are exported from here so the trigger route, the tests and the page read one set.

freeze({repositories, tenantId, kind, details, actor, scope = 'provider', scopeId = 'meta_ads'}) writes the kill-switch row with the REAL resolved tenant_id, never a '' global sentinel, since every query in repositories.js:1-7 binds tenant_id. THE SCOPE PARAMETER EXISTS BECAUSE THE ISSUE NAMES FOUR LEVELS (global, tenant, provider, campaign) AND A SIGNATURE THAT COULD WRITE ONLY ONE DID NOT COVER THEM: scope is one of those four and scope_id is the corresponding id. The default is the provider scope because the demo's only provider is Meta Ads, and it is safe to default to a non-global scope ONLY because killSwitches.activeFor returns every active row for the tenant whatever its scope - the read side was widened to match the write side in the same change, and a test asserts the two agree, so the default can never quietly produce a row no reader can see. It also appends a guardian_incidents row and an audit event through repositories.auditEvents.append({tenant_id, actor, action, subject, details}). Incidents are append-only and never updated: current state is the join with the kill switch, and the banner's kind reads the newest incident by (frozen_at, incident_id), a documented tiebreak because two incidents can share a frozen_at.

reEnable({repositories, tenantId, scope = 'provider', scopeId = 'meta_ads', actor}) REQUIRES an explicit human actor, and with none it is refused RE_ENABLE_ACTOR_REQUIRED. The scope and scopeId defaults are THE SAME LITERALS freeze defaults to, and they are declared here rather than in the route so the two can be compared by a test: a re-enable that named no scope must clear the row the demo's trigger wrote, and a re-enable whose scope does not match the frozen row's clears nothing and reports success, which is the failure mode this default removes. It clears the row and appends an audit event. It does NOT take a recovery predicate.

The ONE documented exception to the actor requirement is resetSeededKillSwitches(tenantId), which clears exactly the row a live trigger writes - scope 'provider', scope_id 'meta_ads' for that tenant - is called only by scripts/seed.js --reset-approvals and is reachable from no route, so the live re-enable path keeps its human-actor invariant.

Beside READ_METHODS (:41-46), add the write half of the provider interface and the one map the executor resolves through. WRITE_METHODS = Object.freeze(['setCampaignStatus', 'updateAdSetBudget', 'updateCampaignCreative', 'createCampaign']) - the four actions ACTION_CLASSES registers, and no more. ACTION_WRITES is a frozen object mapping each registered action name to its method: set_campaign_status -> setCampaignStatus, update_campaign_budget -> updateAdSetBudget, update_campaign_creative -> updateCampaignCreative, create_campaign -> createCampaign. It is keyed by the CONTRACT'S action slugs, not by the JS method names, because the executor looks it up with the capability's SIGNED action string. An action absent from the map is a MALFORMED_CAPABILITY, not a fallthrough to a default. Every write returns the same {ok, ...} envelope the reads use, so the executor has one failure shape to handle: {ok:true, data} on success and {ok:false, error:{code, message, details}} on refusal, with the same codes the read path already returns (META_ERROR_PARAMS' FAILURE_MODES plus the provider's own).

The four WRITE_METHODS, against a per-instance deep copy of FIXTURES rather than the module constant, so a write in one request is not visible in the next - which is what makes AC-2's 'executes exactly once' observable only through the durable store and never through the provider, exactly as the routes.js:103 per-request construction implies. RULES FOR THE WRITES, each one matching a domain rule rather than a convenience: money stays in integer micros, so updateAdSetBudget refuses a non-integer or negative delta_micros and never divides; setCampaignStatus accepts only ACTIVE|PAUSED and the change is visible to the next read on the SAME instance; createCampaign takes {name}, mints the next campaign_00N id, and returns a PAUSED campaign (a new campaign is never born ACTIVE); updateCampaignCreative replaces the creative's name on the named campaign and refuses a campaign the instance does not hold. failureMode applies to WRITES on the same terms as it already applies to reads (:99-115) - quota and revoked refuse with the same codes, messages and simulated details - because the ?meta_error browser clause is a write-path clause and a fake that only failed on reads could not produce it. The deterministic by-id sort the reads already use is applied to every list the writes can change, since FIXTURES is declared out of id order on purpose (:22-25) and a write that appended unsorted would break the contract suite's existing id-order assertion. live.js is NOT required to implement the write interface in this slice and gains no write method: the seam is typed and the live adapter is a later slice, so nothing here commits to a live write contract.

The composition point, and the only place maturity is computed. buildApp gains three optional parameters with pinned defaults - buildApp({repositories, policySecret = DEFAULT_SIGNING_SECRET, policyVersion = '1', capabilityTtlMs = 900_000}) - so the ten existing buildApp call sites (src/index.js:19, test/api/*.test.js, test/web/pages.test.js:227,275,393, test/web/drawer.test.js:22) keep working untouched and a test that needs to forge can pass its own secret. The signing literal is NOT in this file; kernel.js holds it and this file imports DEFAULT_SIGNING_SECRET from there.

ONE PROVIDER HELPER, BECAUSE THE FAILURE-INJECTION CONVENTION MUST NOT BE APPLIED TO ONE WRITE ROUTE AND FORGOTTEN ON THE NEXT. providerForRequest(request) -> new FakeMetaAdsProvider({failureMode: META_ERROR_PARAMS.has(request.query.meta_error) ? request.query.meta_error : 'ok'}), defined once at module level next to META_ERROR_PARAMS (:37). The existing page loop (:100-102) is refactored to call it, and BOTH write routes - POST /v1/approvals/:approvalId/approve and POST /v1/actions/execute - call it and nothing else. This is the defect class the last four rounds each rejected, recurring at a new site: the previous revision named the failureMode source for the execute route and left the approve route saying only 'a provider built for this request', so an implementer following it literally builds the approve route's provider with the default 'ok', the write succeeds, and the failure half of AC-5 can never be observed in a browser - the criterion the recorded rejection was about.

MATURITY, EXTRACTED ONCE. A module-level helper tenantMaturity(repositories, tenantId, nowIso) -> {maturity, band, data_through}, computed from repositories.rawEvents.listByTypes(tenantId, FUNNEL_TYPES) (:43) through dataThrough/maturityFor/policyBand exactly as GET /v1/metrics computes it today (:165-190), with ONE change: a tenant with no events returns maturity: null rather than the 0 the ternary at :174 substitutes. GET /v1/metrics keeps its current wire shape byte for byte by reporting `maturity: maturity ?? 0` and `band: policyBand(maturity ?? 0).label` explicitly, with a comment saying the display surface shows 0 for no data while the gate does not - and test/api/actions.test.js asserts both halves of that in one case, so the two surfaces cannot quietly converge or quietly diverge.

NEW ROUTES, in the order they are mounted (all under the existing app.use('/v1', express.json({strict:true})) at :124, so the 404 envelope at :492-494 still answers anything else):
  POST /v1/capabilities - body {tenant_id, action_class, action, resource, constraints}. Resolves the tenant, builds the intent, calls kernel.validateIntent with {posture: trust.postureFor(...), approval: null, maturity: tenantMaturity(...).maturity} and NOTHING ELSE may mint a capability. 201 {capability_id, envelope, expiry}. A refusal is 403 with the kernel's code and details.
  POST /v1/approvals/:approvalId/approve - the rules run in THIS ORDER, and the order is the contract:
    (0) REDELIVERY. If actionRecords.getByNonce(tenantId, decisionNonce(approvalId)) holds a row, answer 200 {approval_id, status:'executed', executed:false, duplicate:true, receipt_id, reconciliation, drift} and STOP. This rule is FIRST and is deliberately outside the gate: validateIntent refuses an approval row whose status is 'executed' as terminal (kernel rule d), so a duplicate resolved after the gate would 403 forever and the browser clause could never be observed. It is not a second owner of the gate because it mints nothing, issues no capability, calls no provider and mutates no row - it answers about a receipt that already exists. Its doc comment says exactly that. This is the clause the recorded objection required.

    (2) THE ROW. repositories.approvals.get(tenantId, approvalId), else 404 APPROVAL_NOT_FOUND; isPendingApproval(row, {nowIso}) must hold, else 409 APPROVAL_NOT_PENDING with details.status naming the row's real status and whether it lapsed. The tenant comes from body.tenant_id or the row's own tenant, so the page sends what it rendered and a cross-tenant id 404s here rather than executing somebody else's approval.
    (3) THE GATE. kernel.validateIntent with the approval row supplied, exactly as POST /v1/capabilities does; a refusal is 403 with the kernel's code.
    (4) ISSUE AND EXECUTE. issueCapability with nonce: decisionNonce(approvalId) and expiresAtCap: row.expires_at, stored through repositories.capabilities.create, then executor.execute with the provider from providerForRequest(request) - THE SAME HELPER THE EXECUTE ROUTE USES, named here so the omission that broke AC-5 cannot recur.

A provider refusal answers 200 {approval_id, status:'pending', executed:false, duplicate:false, outcome:'provider_refused', error, reconciliation:'unknown'} and writes NO status change - the item stays pending, which is what the criterion asserts. A kill switch answers 409 {code:'KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE'}. A success answers 200 {approval_id, status:'executed', executed:true, receipt_id, reconciliation, drift, band, maturity} and calls repositories.approvals.decide(..., {status:'executed', reason, actor, decided_at}).

It never mints a capability and never touches the executor, so a rejection cannot fail.
  POST /v1/actions/execute - body is a signed envelope. Builds ONE provider through providerForRequest(request) and passes that one instance to the executor for both the write and the re-read. The executor's result maps to HTTP: executed:true -> 200 with the receipt; duplicate -> 200 {executed:false, duplicate:true, receipt_id}; EXECUTION_IN_PROGRESS -> 409 with retryable:true; KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE -> 409; MALFORMED_CAPABILITY -> 400; BAD_SIGNATURE, EXPIRED_CAPABILITY, OVER_SCOPE, TENANT_MISMATCH -> 403.
  POST /v1/guardian/trigger?kind=spend-spike|tracking-loss - runs guardian.evaluate on the tenant's deterministic fixture, and when it trips calls guardian.freeze with the RESOLVED scope (body.scope, body.scope_id, defaulting to guardian.freeze's own defaults, ('provider','meta_ads')). 201 {frozen:true, scope, scope_id, kind, incidents}. An unknown kind is 400 GUARDIAN_KIND_UNKNOWN. It re-arms: a second POST after a re-enable writes the SAME row through the ON CONFLICT upsert and re-freezes, with no database reset, which is what the criterion needs on a re-check.

The response echoes the RESOLVED scope rather than the requested one, so a caller that guessed wrong can see what it actually cleared.
  GET /v1/guardian?tenant_id= - {switches: [...killSwitches.activeFor], incidents: [...guardianIncidents.listForTenant]} so the freeze is readable over the API as well as in the banner. Because activeFor returns every scope for the tenant, this answers with the row the demo's provider-scoped trigger wrote.

NO EXISTING ROUTE CHANGES BEHAVIOUR. The page loop, /v1/events, /v1/metrics, /v1/snapshots, /v1/decisions, /v1/calibration, /v1/learnings, /v1/opportunities, /v1/experiments and both 404 envelopes are untouched, and the last /v1 handler stays last so the new routes are not shadowed.

Automation is frozen ( — ). Approve nothing until a human re-enables it.
`, and nothing at all otherwise, so every existing page test is unaffected. It reads activeFor, which returns every scope for the tenant, so the provider-scoped row the demo writes shows the banner. APPROVALS SCREEN, TWO SOURCES, and which is which is stated because the previous revision read everything from one and could not have rendered a receipt. risks: This is a fourteen-file change that creates a write path, a trust ledger, a kill switch and a live approvals screen in one ticket, and the whole of it is new surface in the highest-risk part of the system. Nothing here is a refactor of something that already works; the only pre-existing behaviour at risk is the approvals screen and the dashboard's guardian panel, both of which are being replaced.

The three blocking defects this work order corrects were all the same shape as the ones the last four rounds were rejected for - an assertion with no mechanism behind it - and they were each found by re-reading the same files, not by new insight. A fourth round finding in the same family is therefore plausible, and the review stage on this route is where it should be caught.

POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface whose only control is the signing secret, and that secret has a public dev default. A capability forged offline is accepted without the trust ledger ever being consulted, and the blast radius is bounded only by the fact that the only writable provider is an in-memory fake.

A ticket branch may not write .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md or environment.md, so those stay stale about the new data-testids, the new /v1 routes and the --reset-approvals re-run contract until the Librarian's branch is refreshed. qa_script is a substitute for them, not a replacement.

WAL is a new on-disk format for every existing ./data/app.db and leaves -wal/-shm sidecars. The seed process and the server both open the file, and a QA run that copies or inspects data/app.db directly will find a database whose committed content lives partly in the sidecar. The remedy for a stale schema is still to delete ./data/app.db with the server stopped; with WAL, delete the sidecars too.
out_of_scope: Automatic or deterministic-policy re-enable of a freeze. The deterministic half - guardian.recoveryHolds - is exported, named and tested; nothing in this slice calls it, because the seeded spend spike is produced by evaluating static seed data and never subsides, so enforcing it would make AC-3's re-enable permanently unreachable. A later slice wires it to the machine-side evaluator.
Any live write against the Meta Graph API. live.js gains no write method: the write interface is typed and the fake is the only implementation, so this slice commits to no live write contract.

Writing trust_ledger rows in production. The ledger's writer is strategy code in a later slice; this slice only seeds calibration fixtures and reads them. Both the rendered table and the gate read the same rows, so a row that appears later moves both.

Rejecting two concurrent approvals for the same action_class and resource. Nothing in this slice proposes actions, so duplicate proposals are a later slice's concern; today both execute, and test/executor/executor.test.js asserts that rather than leaving it implicit.

Account-specific maturity bands. BAND_ORDER is exported and pinned against policyBand's current output, so a re-ordering fails loudly rather than quietly inverting the floor, but which band each class should require is a calibration question this slice cannot settle from the code.
Clearing the ?meta_error simulation from the page. It is a URL-level switch with no on-page indicator, pre-existing on /, and unchanged here.

Correcting docs/trd.md's TR-7 '>0.90 strategic' to the '>= 0.90' the implementation and its pinned test use. docs/** is out of bounds from a ticket branch; the implementation wins and the drift is reported here instead.

A DOM or JS-execution test harness for src/web/client.js. The repo has none and adding one is out of proportion for a single vanilla IIFE; the invariants that matter - the confirm, the retry safety, the meta_error forwarding, the three-way response branch - were moved to the server or asserted over HTTP, and the remainder is stated in residual_risks as qa_script-only rather than implied to be covered.

IAC-6 through any further IAC-n the split recorded and this work order does not name: the issue body is not readable from this repository, so the split's full acceptance list could not be checked against the criteria above. The five IAC-n carried in the criteria are covered; if the split recorded more, each needs either a criterion here or its own issue.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep new-geography row-less as an earlier proposal specified, and change AC-6, qa_script and the test case to 'new-geography approval-required and labelled policy-only'
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would leave NO class on seed data rendering 'shadow', and the posture table exists to demonstrate the posture ladder, so that resolution deletes the rung the table is asking to see. The stated resolution keeps all four rungs visible on seed data; the cost is that the seed, not the criterion, is what changes.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give creative-refresh a scored row so it renders 'approval-required' instead of pinned shadow, and keep new-geography as the only shadow class
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It produces the same five rendered rows but makes two high-risk classes' postures depend on precision thresholds computed from four and two observations. A pinned row is the honest statement for a class that should never be autonomous regardless of what the ledger says.

alternatives_considered.approach: Render a no-row class as a fourth posture label, 'no evidence', so the fail-closed rung is visible in column 2 rather than in the Why prose
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It breaks the three-label invariant AC-6 asserts, and it conflates a class with no evidence about it and a class with evidence saying approval required. Both fail closed, but only one has ever been measured.

alternatives_considered.approach: Defer autonomous execution within micro-limits: add it to out_of_scope and rewrite AC-4 to verify only the posture table
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The issue's out_of_scope defers only 'autonomous strategic actions BEYOND micro-limits', so micro-limit autonomy is in scope and IAC-4's verb is 'executes'. A display-only check passes on a plan where the ledger is inert, which is the exact 'looks finished while shipping' shape, and would leave a trust ledger with no reader for a later slice to rediscover.

alternatives_considered.approach: Move the posture check into the executor as well as at issuance, so /v1/actions/execute is also gated on the ledger
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Two owners for one check, and the second is wrong: a trust row edited between issuance and execution would retroactively invalidate a correctly signed capability, so a legitimate write would fail for a reason the signer cannot see. validateIntent is the single gate and a signed capability is the attestation; the executor re-checks only what can change underneath a capability - signature, expiry, scope, tenant, kill switch. The asymmetry is accepted and stated in files[] and residual_risks rather than papered over.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give the kernel a mutating {claim(nonce)} port and let it reject a replay before the executor's action_records lookup
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This contradicts AC-2: the second delivery would get an error envelope instead of the original receipt, and the kernel has no way to produce a receipt_id. The executor dedupes and claims first, the kernel's port stays read-only {seen}, and both criteria hold.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the executor's dedupe as a bare read of action_records by nonce, with no atomic claim
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is what an earlier proposal specified and it does not close what the plan says it closes. Two deliveries that interleave - two tabs, a retried POST against a slow provider - both pass the read and both reach the provider. The repository already ships claim/record/release and the scheduler uses exactly that shape, so the fix is a reuse rather than a new mechanism.

alternatives_considered.approach: Move signature and expiry validation ahead of the executor's duplicate lookup, so an unsigned POST naming a guessed nonce learns nothing
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is a fair hardening and it stays in residual_risks, but it is not free: AC-2 requires a duplicate made while a kill switch is active to return the original receipt rather than 409, and validateCapability is what raises the kill-switch refusal. Splitting signature-before and kill-switch-after would give validateCapability two entry points in a module whose whole design claim is one owner for the gate. The property at stake is a read-only receipt id behind a nonce that a caller would have to guess, on a surface whose only writable provider is an in-memory fake.

alternatives_considered.approach: Move the dev-default signing literal into a new src/policy/secret.js and have both index.js and routes.js import it
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It resolves a contradiction but makes src/api/routes.js import a signing constant from src/policy/, which is the very clause the isolation test uses to say routes.js does not hold key material. Keeping the literal in kernel.js and importing it as a value keeps index.js the only reader of the environment variable and keeps the isolation test's meaning intact.

alternatives_considered.approach: Let the maturity helper keep the metric route's 0-hours substitution for a tenant with no events, and rely on the kernel's finite-number guard alone
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A no-data tenant is handed a legitimate 0 before the kernel ever sees an absent value, and 0 is the emergency-only band, which every seeded class requires - so a brand-new tenant would execute autonomously with a healthy-looking band. That contradicts the fail-closed claim, and the fix is one line in a helper this change is already writing.

alternatives_considered.approach: Let validateIntent read the approvals and raw-events repositories directly instead of taking the approval row and maturity as arguments
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would make the policy kernel impure and break the import-boundary test - the kernel exists to be a deterministic pure function. It would also make the maturity SOURCE implicit, which is the defect this work order fixes: the source is named in one place, the route, and pinned by a test.

alternatives_considered.approach: JWT library (jose) for capability signing
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A new runtime dependency for what node:crypto's createHmac with timingSafeEqual does in a few lines; conventions require stdlib first with a one-line justification and there is none to give.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep one pending approval fixture and rewrite the script to approve the same still-pending item twice
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes a browser criterion depend on a subtle two-step order on one item, and a QA run that succeeds on the first click leaves nothing to fail on the second. Two distinct fixtures satisfy both orderings and give the posture table its executed and lapsed sections for free.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep a '' sentinel tenant_id for the global kill switch and give the reader a special two-scope read
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It needs a deliberate exception to the module contract at src/data/repositories.js:1-7, and a reader who misses the exception silently loses the global freeze. A global-scope row carrying a real tenant_id, read by the same tenant-bound query as everything else, needs no exception at all - and 'every active row for this tenant' is what activeFor now does, which also covers the provider and campaign scopes the issue names.

alternatives_considered.approach: Freeze at scope 'global' so the existing two-disjunct activeFor read finds the row, instead of widening activeFor
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes the demo exercise the one scope whose semantics do not need testing. The four levels the issue names are only meaningful if a provider-scoped freeze is written and a provider-scoped write is refused, which is the case widening activeFor enables and defaulting to 'global' would hide. The read side was widened instead, and a test pins that the two sides agree.

alternatives_considered.approach: Let issueCapability overwrite the envelope's action from ACTION_CLASSES instead of refusing a mis-paired intent
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It closes the hole silently: a caller who asks to spend campaign-status autonomy on a campaign creation gets a signed capability for a status change and no error, and the mismatch is invisible everywhere downstream. Refusal makes it a 403 with a named reason, costs one rule, and is testable from outside the module.

alternatives_considered.approach: Enforce the deterministic recovery predicate on the live re-enable route, and require the QA script to re-seed the baseline before re-enabling
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The seeded spend spike is produced by evaluating static seed data, so it never subsides and an enforced predicate makes AC-3's re-enable permanently unreachable - the criterion would be asserted and unobservable. IAC-3 asks for explicit human OR deterministic-policy re-enable; the human half is the live route's job, the predicate is the machine half's, and automatic re-enable is filed in out_of_scope with the reason.

alternatives_considered.approach: Enforce the deterministic recovery predicate at the repository level as an option the route never sets
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is the same shape as a fold function this plan already refuses to ship with no caller: a boolean nobody sets, which makes a safety property look enforced while nothing enforces it. The predicate is exported and tested by name, and its one honest consumer is the machine-side evaluator a later slice will add.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give the executed-receipts panel its data by adding receipt_id, reconciliation and drift columns to the approvals table, so partitionApprovals alone can render it
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It duplicates the receipt on a working-state row and leaves two answers for one fact: the receipt appended by the executor and the copy written by the page's read path can disagree, and the executor is the only writer that can be trusted to have run. The panel reads action_records, which is where the values were written.

alternatives_considered.approach: Show the executed section from actionRecords.listForTenant with no approval_id filter, so an autonomous execution appears in the approvals audit trail too
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes qa_script step 12's 'ZERO executed receipts' false on the second run of the script: the step-9 autonomous receipt has a null approval_id, is not in the reset's purge list, and would sit in a panel that otherwise counts decisions taken on this queue. Filtering to approval-backed receipts keeps the count the script asserts, and the autonomous execution is still audited in audit_events.

alternatives_considered.approach: Drop the trust_ledger PRIMARY KEY and resolve a class's posture by 'the most recent row wins'
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Not seriously considered: the key is already pinned in the migration and the reason for it - one displayed posture and one enforced posture read from one row - is the property this design exists to provide. Recorded because the critique raised it, so the dismissal is on the record rather than silent.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give the reset a disposable database per QA run instead of deleting rows from the live one
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The server holds ./data/app.db open for its process lifetime, so unlinking or replacing the file leaves QA talking to a server reading a deleted inode. The alternative the plan rejected for the same reason - a reset epoch in the nonce - is recorded in residual_risks as what a later slice could adopt if receipts ever need to be genuinely undeletable.

assumptions: The QA harness owns the server boot (.sdlc/config.yml:107 env.boot = npm run sdlc:serve) and can run `npm run sdlc:seed -- --reset-approvals` against the same ./data/app.db the running server has open, without unlinking the file and without restarting the server. The script entry is `node scripts/seed.js` (package.json:13) and the module has no flag parsing today, so the flag is read from process.argv and npm passes it through with `--`; if the harness cannot pass extra argv the same reset is reachable as `node scripts/seed.js --reset-approvals`. This is the assumption every browser criterion depends on and it is the one thing that cannot be verified from the code. What the code DOES settle: PRAGMA busy_timeout is per-connection, so placing it in openDatabase covers both the server and the seed process, and qa_script step 1 states the expected busy text so a lock is distinguishable from an empty queue.

Maturity for the gate is the tenant's data-through age computed over FUNNEL_TYPES-filtered raw events through the repo's own dataThrough/maturityFor/policyBand, in one helper extracted from GET /v1/metrics. On seed data the journey events are stamped by occurredAt() at scripts/seed.js:381, about six hours before the run, so maturity is about 0.0625 and reads 'emergency-only', which every seeded class requires and is therefore admitted. A tenant with NO events is not admitted at all: the helper returns null and the kernel refuses it as 'maturity-unknown'.

The approve path supplies the approval row it is executing to validateIntent, so a non-autonomous class is admitted by an explicit human approval and refused without one, and an autonomous class is admitted whether or not a row is supplied. IAC-4's 'new-geography stays in shadow or approval' is read as sanctioning exactly this: shadow means never autonomous, approval means a human may still say yes. This is also why the page renders no disabled approve button - a control that says 'you may not approve this' would contradict the rule the server enforces.

The seed's trust-ledger numbers (6/6/0/0 autonomous, 3/2/1/0 approval-required, two pinned shadow, one class with no row) are calibration fixtures chosen by this plan, and they are what make the enforced posture and the displayed posture agree. If a human wants different numbers the gate changes with them; what must not happen is the two surfaces being derived from different data, which is why both read trust.postureFor over the same rows and a test asserts the rendered table against the gate's own verdict.

An approval is created by strategy code in a later slice; this slice only decides, executes and records, so the seed and the tests are the only approval writers. This is also why nothing in this change can detect two pending approvals for the same resource - no component here proposes, so the duplicate case is deferred rather than solved.

A signed capability is valid on its own authority for its whole lifetime and is not re-checked against the trust ledger at execute time (see alternatives_considered for why a second owner is worse). One consequence is chosen rather than discovered: a capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch. That is recorded in residual_risks rather than left to be found.

The browser sends the tenant it rendered a card from, as data-tenant-id on the control and tenant_id in the decide body. resolveTenantId already accepts an explicit tenant and otherwise falls back to the sole tenant, or to 'tenant_demo' when two or more exist - so without this the moment a second tenant exists every browser decision 404s on a row that is genuinely pending, while the cross-tenant 404 test still passes and gives false confidence.

'meta_ads' is the only provider scope id this epic has, because Meta Ads is the only integration in it. The provider key in the kernel's four-scope check is written as a named constant for that reason; when a second provider is integrated, the check becomes a loop over a provider list and the constant becomes its first entry.
unknowns: Whether the running server holds a write lock on ./data/app.db at the moment the reset runs. If it does, busy_timeout converts an immediate failure into a five-second wait and the reset may still fail; the reset's printed summary is what tells the two apart, which is why step 1 reads it.

Whether the QA harness passes extra arguments through `npm run sdlc:seed --` to the node process, or invokes `node scripts/seed.js --reset-approvals` directly. The flag is parsed from process.argv either way, so both work, but the qa_script names the npm form and a harness that rewrites it would need the node form.

Whether anything outside the repository (a CI step, the harness's own config) already writes to approvals, capabilities, action_records or kill_switches under other names. Nothing in this repository does, which is all that could be checked from here.
The exact Graph mutation endpoints and field names a live write would use. Deliberately untouched: live.js gains no write method, so no write contract beyond the typed shapes is committed to here.

How a real provider reports drift source. The fake reports it from its own simulation and the executor classifies whatever the provider names; against a live provider this needs a platform-side signal this slice does not have.

Whether any band edge will move as account-specific bands replace the default lag model (TR-7's 'bands become account-specific over time'). BAND_ORDER is exported and pinned against policyBand's current output in a test, so a re-ordering would fail loudly rather than quietly invert the floor - but the right band per class is a calibration question this slice cannot settle from the code.

The full list of IAC-n the split recorded for this issue. The issue body is not readable from this repository, so the criteria here could be checked only against the five IAC ids the previous rounds carried. If the split recorded more, each needs a criterion here or its own issue; that is stated in out_of_scope rather than assumed complete.
residual_risks: QA reads these first. (1) The provider-failure clause depends on both write routes calling one shared providerForRequest helper. That is now named in both, and a test asserts the approve route's ?meta_error=quota refusal over HTTP, so the two cannot drift - but the browser half of it still has no automated coverage and is qa_script step 5 only.

(2) The kill-switch clause depends on the write and read sides agreeing about scopes. activeFor now returns every scope for the tenant, freeze and reEnable share one pair of default literals, and a test asserts the agreement - but the four-scope enforcement is unit-tested through an injected port, and only the provider-scoped case is ever driven live.

(3) POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface whose only control is the signing secret, and the secret has a public dev default, so a capability forged offline is accepted without the trust ledger ever being consulted; the blast radius is bounded only by the fact that the only writable provider is the in-memory fake.

(4) The executor's duplicate lookup runs BEFORE signature validation, deliberately, so that a redelivery under an active kill switch returns its receipt rather than a 409. The cost is that an unsigned POST naming a guessed nonce gets a receipt id back with no write performed.

(5) The two-step confirm, the retry safety, the meta_error forwarding and the three-way response branch are enforced SERVER-side because the repo has no DOM harness; the REST of client.js - the in-flight guard, the toast fill, the pending-count decrement, the reason input surviving a failure - has NO executable coverage and is verified by qa_script steps 3-7 only. Read those assertions as human observation, not as a regression net.
(6) The signing secret's dev default is live wherever POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET is unset, which today is everywhere.

(7) .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md and environment.md are NOT updated by this work order - a ticket branch may not touch them - and qa_script is a substitute, not a replacement. They stay stale about the new data-testids (guardian-banner, posture-table, posture-row-<action_class>, approval-card, approval-queue, approval-executed, executed-receipt, approval-lapsed, lapsed-row, approval-toast, approval-failed, approval-already-decided, approval-decision-result), the new /v1 routes and the --reset-approvals re-run contract until the Librarian's branch is refreshed.
(8) A capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch; nothing records that the capability predates the freeze.
(9) Two pending approvals for the same action_class and resource both execute - correct for this slice, since nothing here proposes, and asserted so a future dedupe is deliberate.

(10) No seeded class requires a band above 'emergency-only', so the live demo never exercises the maturity floor in its restrictive direction: it is covered by test/policy/kernel.test.js with explicit maturity fixtures, and a change to the band thresholds or to a class's requiredMaturityBand would NOT redden the live demo - only the kernel suite notices. The same is true of the micro-limits.

(11) The only drift value reachable in a live QA run is 'none', because the fake reports drift from an injected writeDrift option; manual, platform and third-party are unit-tested only. AC-2's 'the receipt carries the drift' is therefore half-live.

(12) The concurrent-decision loser is answered EXECUTION_IN_PROGRESS with retryable:true and lands in client.js's failure branch, so for the seconds while the winner is in flight that branch's 'nothing was executed' is literally true but reads like a failure. The server's own retryable message is shown beneath it, which is the mitigation; it is not a fourth panel.

(13) A kill switch raised between a page load and a click is enforced server-side but not reflected in the already-rendered page, so an operator can see a clean queue and be refused. The server is the authority and the banner is a convenience; a live indicator would need polling, which this slice does not add.

(14) A tenant with zero funnel events sees a 403 MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED on a card the page rendered as approvable, with no page-side signal that the account has no data yet. The posture table shows the classes but nothing ties the 403 to it.

(15) A local database may carry a stale 006 from an earlier revision of this issue and keep its old table shape while the migration reads as applied, because every statement is IF NOT EXISTS. The remedy is to delete ./data/app.db - and, now that WAL is on, its -wal and -shm sidecars - with the server stopped.

(16) A QA run that begins more than 24 hours after the last reset finds the three pending fixtures lapsed too, and every approval returns 409. The reset re-stamps them, which is why it is step 1; a run that skips it is not re-runnable for this reason alone.

(17) The action_records DELETE allowance is enforced by a test, not by a schema rule. A later slice that seeds a differently-named approval, or widens the deletion, reintroduces exactly the second-run failure the two-group reset stamp fixed, and nothing else in the suite would notice.

(18) The back-button case: client.js reloads the queue from the server after a success rather than removing the card optimistically, which is the right call, and the re-decide control is the truthful answer to a bfcache-rendered page landing with buttons still armed on a card that is already executed. What is not covered is back after a FAILURE panel: the typed reason lives only in the input, so a back/forward pair re-renders the queue from the server and the unsaved reason is gone. That is ordinary browser behaviour for unsaved form state, not a defect, and no test asserts either way.

(19) The dashboard's guardian panel now lists incidents, so the sentence 'No guardian incidents in the last 24 hours.' survives only in the no-incidents branch - which is the branch a seeded-but-unfrozen database takes. A test or QA note that matched that sentence as a literal will still match, and should not be read as the panel being unchanged.

(20) The posture table's first column now reads roster slugs ('campaign-status') where it read prose ('Campaign status change'), and the new-geography and campaign-launch rows both read approval-required with different Why copy. Nothing asserts the prose, so no test catches a future copy regression; the change is recorded here for the Librarian to reconcile against docs/ui.md.

(21) The five-state shells, the 404 envelope for unknown /v1 paths and the fake provider's cross-request statelessness are contracts this change edits or extends; test/web/approvals.test.js, test/api/*.test.js and test/integrations/meta_ads.test.js cover them explicitly, so read those assertions as the regression net rather than trusting this description.

(22) The null-scope posture table - five rows, all approval required, no evidence - is what a tenantless database renders, and the null-tenant guardian banner returns an empty string. It is the fail-closed answer and it keeps the existing page suite green, but it is a screen nobody has looked at, because the seeded demo never has a null scope.
approved_work_order.confidence_rationale: The root cause is verified against the repository and not in doubt: there is no src/policy/, no src/executor/, no guardian, MIGRATIONS closes at 005, openDatabase sets no PRAGMA, createRepositories builds exactly thirteen repositories, and the approvals page is the static shell both prior documents describe. The three blocking defects this work order corrects I re-checked myself, at the lines the critique cited, and all three hold: routes.js:37 and :100-102 confirm the failure-injection convention has exactly one consumer today and the approve route named none; the write side defaults freeze to ('provider','meta_ads') while activeFor was specified over only the global and tenant disjuncts, so the row the demo writes was invisible to the banner, to GET /v1/guardian and to every other reader, and the envelope carries no scope for the four-key kill-switch check to read; and the reset re-stamped all four fixtures to now+24h while resetToSeed returns every one of them to status 'pending', so the lapsed fixture came back pending and step 2 of the QA script contradicted step 1 of the same script. Each is a naming defect rather than a design error, and each is now closed with a mechanism and a test case behind it. What holds the number at 71 rather than in the eighties is two things, neither of them a guess about the design. First, the base rate: this is the fifth round, the last four were each rejected for the same family - an assertion with no mechanism behind it - and the critique found three more instances of it in v13 plus five majors, all of them found by re-reading the same files rather than by any new insight about the problem. A fourth round finding in that family is plausible and should be priced in rather than argued away, and it is why I did not simply carry the proposal's own 74 forward. Second, the one thing that gates every browser criterion - whether the QA harness can pass --reset-approvals to a seed process writing to a database the running server holds open - cannot be verified from the code at all, and a fail there makes the whole browser half observable once per database. The diff is also fourteen files and four new modules, large relative to how much of it any single test touches. What would move it up: an implementer writing test/policy/kernel.test.js and test/api/approvals.test.js first and finding that the band floor, the finite-and-null maturity refusals, the four-scope kill-switch check, the autonomous-plus-approval case, the action binding, the atomic claim, the receipt-before-status ordering, the three-way response branch and the two-group reset stamp all hold together. What would move it down: QA discovering it cannot reset against the live server's open handle, or a second tenant appearing in a demo database and 404ing every browser decision.
approved_work_order.debate_summary:
The critique was right more often than not, and I am not going to dress that up. I re-checked every finding against the file and line it cited, and I confirmed all nine against the code rather than accepting the citations. Three blocking findings hold and all three are folded in with the mechanism named, plus five majors. The first blocker is the same defect the previous round was corrected for, recurring one route over: the proposal named the failureMode source for POST /v1/actions/execute and left the approve route saying only 'a provider built for this request', so an implementer following it literally builds that provider with the default 'ok', the write succeeds, and the failure half of AC-5 - the clause the recorded rejection was about - can never be observed. I went past the critique's suggestion and made it one providerForRequest(request) helper that the page loop and both write routes call, so the convention has a single home and a third route cannot forget it. The second blocker is new to this round and is a regression the proposal introduced: v12 defaulted freeze to scope 'global', which the two-disjunct activeFor read actually matched; v13 changed the default to ('provider','meta_ads') to exercise a real level of the four the issue names, and left activeFor over only global and tenant rows. The row the demo writes is therefore invisible to the banner, to GET /v1/guardian and to the test that asserts the freeze is readable - AC-3 unobservable end to end - and the same gap leaves the kernel's isActive port with no caller, since the envelope carries no scope. I widened the read to every scope bound to the tenant rather than narrowing the write back to global, because defaulting to 'global' would make the demo exercise the one scope whose semantics need no testing, and I named the four scope keys the check evaluates so OVER_SCOPE and KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE have a defined path. The third blocker is a self-inflicted one: the reset re-stamped all four fixtures to now+24h while resetToSeed returns every one of them to status 'pending', so the lapsed fixture came back pending. Since step 1 IS the reset, every run failed at step 2. The fix restores the two groups differently - three pending at now+24h, the lapsed one at its original past stamp - and makes the summary print the two counts separately so '4 rows restored' is never read as '4 pending'.
